subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: What it is and why it matters.

blocks.html:
Your phone knows more about you than any other device: where you go, who you talk to, your photos, your health and your money. Much of that is shared with apps, advertisers and your carrier by default. A few settings — app permissions, location history, the advertising ID and a strong passcode — make a big difference, whatever phone you have.

The operating system is the foundation everything else runs on, so it decides how much you can protect at all. Windows, macOS, Android and iOS all collect some data about how you use them; some let you turn most of it off, and Linux-based systems collect very little to begin with. Whatever you use, keeping it updated is the single most important security habit.

subsections.title: Terminology
subsections.summary: The words you will run into.

items.title: App permissions
items.html: What an app is allowed to access: location, camera, microphone, contacts. Grant only what it needs.

items.title: Advertising ID
items.html: An identifier apps use to track you for ads. Delete or reset it in settings.

items.title: Biometric unlock
items.html: Face or fingerprint unlock. Convenient, but in some places you can be forced to use it.

items.title: Full-disk encryption
items.html: Scrambles everything on the phone until it is unlocked with your passcode.

items.title: IMSI catcher
items.html: A fake cell tower that tricks nearby phones into connecting so they can be tracked.

items.title: Telemetry
items.html: Usage and diagnostic data an OS sends back to its maker.

items.title: Linux distribution
items.html: A complete operating system built on the Linux kernel, such as Debian, Fedora or Ubuntu.

items.title: Open source
items.html: Software whose code anyone can read, so its behaviour can be checked independently.

items.title: Security update
items.html: A patch for a known hole. Attackers target unpatched systems first.

items.title: Disk encryption
items.html: BitLocker, FileVault or LUKS — makes your data unreadable if the device is stolen.
